# Diagnosing High Fuel Consumption in the 2008 Nissan Altima 2.5S

A vehicle burning half a tank of fuel over just 50 miles on an 80% highway run is a clear symptom of significant inefficiency. The 2008 Nissan Altima 2.5S, equipped with the QG25DE 2.5-liter inline-four engine and CVT transmission, has a known history of fuel consumption issues that often stem from specific mechanical or electronic control unit (ECU) behaviors rather than generic wear. When a car with 164k miles presents this symptom after a month of normal operation, the troubleshooting process must move beyond basic maintenance checks like tire pressure and air filter cleaning, which you have already verified.

The first technical suspect in this specific model year is the variable intake manifold system. The QG25DE engine utilizes a VIM (Variable Intake Manifold) that alters valve timing to optimize torque at different RPMs. On older examples with high mileage, the actuator motor responsible for switching between low and high lift cam profiles can fail or bind. If the ECU commands the manifold into a specific configuration for performance but the mechanical linkage gets stuck in a suboptimal position, the engine runs inefficiently, causing immediate fuel penalty. This is a hardware failure that requires physical inspection of the actuator arm and the vacuum lines connected to it, not just an OBDII scan.

A second critical area to investigate involves the throttle body and idle air control logic. The 2008 Altima relies on a drive-by-wire system where the ECU learns the throttle plate position via an adaptive learning process. Over time, carbon buildup around the throttle bore or a faulty idle motor can prevent the valve from seating correctly when the pedal is released. If the engine cannot maintain idle stability without opening the throttle slightly wider than necessary, fuel consumption spikes dramatically on highways because the ECU compensates for perceived low load conditions by enriching the mixture. Resetting the throttle body adaptation by disconnecting the battery for 15 minutes can sometimes clear these learned values and force the ECU to relearn the baseline, though this is a temporary fix if carbon buildup is severe.

The continuously variable transmission (CVT) in this generation also plays a role in fuel economy. Unlike traditional automatics with fixed gear ratios, the CVT keeps the engine in its power band. If the transmission control module detects slippage or overheating in the belt and pulley system, it may default to a "limp mode" strategy that locks the ratio at a higher RPM than optimal for cruising. This behavior drastically reduces miles per gallon. Since you noted no external leaks, internal pressure loss or clutch pack wear within the transmission could be forcing the engine to work harder to maintain highway speeds.

Finally, consider the oxygen sensors and fuel trim data. The ECU constantly adjusts the air-fuel ratio based on feedback from upstream and downstream O2 sensors. If a sensor is providing erroneous lean readings, the ECU will inject more fuel than required to compensate. Using an OBDII scanner to check long-term fuel trims (LTFT) is essential here; if LTFT values are consistently positive (e.g., +10% or higher), it indicates the engine is running rich due to sensor error or vacuum leaks elsewhere in the intake system that haven't been visually detected.

If hardware inspections and software adaptations fail to resolve the issue, replacing the VIM actuator or inspecting the CVT for belt slip becomes the next logical step before considering a full engine rebuild.
